The original base program was funded through an internal city loan of 2.5 million plus 250,000 in capital funding for administration.

This funding was then leveraged to apply for FCM funding, which was approved in 2022 providing 7.3 million in loans to be distributed to program participants and 3.6 million of grants to be used for rebates and program enhancements.
This report and presentation provides a status update on helps performance over the first year.

It explains the upcoming enhancements expected to be launched in 2023 and then goes through recommended program improvements and associated by law amendments that require city council review and approval. Next slide please.
As of January 5, 2023, the program had received over 478 applications, not 487 as it says on the slide. Sorry about that error, but we do continue to receive applications all the time.
Of these 478, roughly 257 are expected to be able to participate in the program. 45 of these have voluntarily been removed or were intelligible and that leaves about 182 households on the way list.

Of that 257 that are in the program, 33 have completed their retrofits, 58 are in progress, 12 have submitted their funding requests and are working through that process and 141 haven't yet submitted funding requests.
There is also 13 that have just recently been moved from the way list into the program.

About 26% of the projects in progress are completed are from income qualified households and on average participants are doing multiple upgrades with their help loans with an average loan amount of $31,600.
Next slide please.
As you can see, the most popular upgrades are the window and door replacements followed by furnace replacement and air conditioner install.
Addict insulation and water heat replacement are almost as popular as furnace and AC replacement.
Some of the upgrades that are increasing in popularity in recent months include air source heat pumps, insulation, air ceiling and solar PB.
Next slide please.
The city commissioned an economic impact report from SREDA to estimate the total impacts of the program on the local economy.
Tyler new in from SREDA is available today to answer any specific questions that the committee members might have about the SREDA study, which is also attached to the admin report.

In brief, SREDA reported that during the first year of the program, 289 upgrades were completed and that is projected to result in about 19.43 million in total economic output over the life of the program.
It is also expected to lead to 90 jobs over the full program and save residents $20,211 per year in energy costs.
This amounts to about 283 tons of CO2 per year.
Or roughly the same amount of GHGs as driving 61 gas powered vehicles for a year.
Next slide please.
Each help participant is required to do a pre-imposed energy audit by certified energy advisor.
On average, before retrofits, each home emitted approximately 13.2 tons of CO2 per year.
And as you can see on this slide, one ton of CO2-E would fill a cube 8.13 meters high, so taller than your average house.
With help retrofits, we saw about a 20% decrease in GHG emissions on average, saving approximately 2.6 tons of CO2-E per year.
Next slide, after each participant completes a project through the program, they are sent to survey and the results are compiled by FCM.
So far, we've only had five participants complete the survey.
However, participants do provide regular feedback to our program coordinator on the application process, so we are constantly receiving feedback and adjusting our program.
Based on the survey feedback, 80% were satisfied with the program overall.
75% would not have completed their retrofits without the support of the program.
75% noted that they noticed a big improvement in energy use, and 50% said they would recommend it to a friend. Next slide please.
Program enhancements are currently being designed and procured. These new tools will be targeted to all residential homeowners in Saskatoon, not just those participating in help.

Help is addressing the financial barrier to energy retrofits, while enhancements can begin to address the knowledge and implementation barriers for homeowners, so they can be coach through the renovation process.

Educated about what they may not know is the best bang for their bucks for home retrofits and be empowered to make decisions that will reduce energy and emissions for the community. Next slide please.
Program enhancements include the residential solar potential map. This is a searchable map that shows a home solar potential cost and payback.
And that should be launched right away in March.
The residential energy map in digital concertage is a searchable map that shows a digital energy label for each house.
Complete with home upgrade upgrades suggestions based on the age and archetype of the house, as well as cost and payback estimates.

Energy coaching service is a service where residents can request an energy coach to complete a virtual or an in person walk through of their house to help determine what energy upgrades would be most beneficial.
Residents can also call a general hotline to talk to an energy coach to answer all types of energy retrofit questions.
The real estate agent training program is currently under development in partnership with the Saskatchewan Realtors Association.
This training program will help build knowledge and demand in the real estate agent in the real estate industry for energy efficient homes.
Finally all the programs will be supported by a multi-faceted communications campaign that will build awareness of energy efficiency options for residential homes.
We've met by some of the common misconceptions and promote the new tools and services mentioned above.

Next, the non-responsive participants.

approximately half of these are not responding to emails about whether they plan to participate in the program or not.
A bylaw amendment is recommended to implement a deadline of six months for participants to provide project information or be removed from the program.
Next, eligible residences.
Currently, condominium buildings, even if they are detached semi-detached or row-style condos, are not eligible for the program.
However, the archetype of detached semi-detached and row-housing style condos is similar to single-family households, and is allowable under the FCM rules for inclusion.
Therefore, we recommend amending the bylaw to allow them to participate.
Large multi-level and multi-unit condo buildings would still be ineligible for help.
As these buildings fit better within the institutional industrial and commercial building energy retrofit program, which is in development.
Next slide, please.
